aliases.name: Konoha-tengu

description.summary: Japanese supernatural creatures depicted as bird-like or humanoid mountain spirits. Originally portrayed as Buddhist demons, later evolved into protective mountain guardians. Masters of martial arts, flight, and shape-shifting.
description.full: Tengu are one of the most iconic creatures in Japanese folklore, supernatural beings that inhabit mountains and forests. They exist in two primary forms: Karasu-tengu (crow-like with bird heads) and Konoha-tengu (humanoid with red faces and distinctive long noses). Originally depicted as malevolent Buddhist demons who led people astray, tengu evolved over centuries into complex figures serving as mountain guardians and martial arts masters. They are known for their pride and arrogance, supernatural powers including flight and shape-shifting, and their role in teaching legendary warriors. Tengu remain deeply embedded in Japanese culture through Shinto shrines, folklore, martial arts mythology, and modern media.

origins.cultural_roots: Derived from Chinese tiangou (heavenly dog) but developed distinctly in Japanese Buddhism and Shinto. Associated with yamabushi mountain ascetics and Buddhist corruption narratives.
origins.earliest_accounts: First mentioned in Nihon Shoki (720 CE) as a celestial omen. Evolved through medieval Buddhist tales.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to Buddhist concepts of pride and arrogance as spiritual obstacles, later integrated with Shinto mountain worship.

history.modern_era: Tengu remain active in Japanese culture through Shinto shrines dedicated to tengu worship, annual festivals, martial arts mythology (particularly in kenjutsu and ninjutsu traditions), and widespread representation in anime, manga, and video games. They serve as symbols of mountain guardianship and martial discipline.

folklore.beliefs: Tengu embody both danger and wisdom. They punish arrogance but reward humility and dedication. Associated with supernatural martial mastery.

religious.significance: Originally Buddhist demons representing spiritual obstacles (pride, anger). Later integrated into Shinto as mountain kami guardians.
religious.sensitivity_note: ⚠️ CULTURAL SENSITIVITY: Tengu are part of living Japanese religious and cultural traditions. Approach with respect for Shinto and Buddhist contexts.
religious.respect_guidelines: Recognize religious significance in shrine contexts. Do not trivialize or appropriate sacred imagery. Consult Japanese cultural experts for accurate representation.
